transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Hale (Redwood AE), Sofia Liang (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (BrightScale CTO), Priya Kapoor (BrightScale ML Infra), Evan Park (BrightScale SRE)

Summary / Goals: Deep technical dive to tune throughput on Redwood Dedicated for BrightScale's realtime enrichment pipeline. Focus: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache and quantization impact.

[00:00] Marcus: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to walk through the tuning knobs we discussed in the doc and make sure we've got an action plan for the pilot, uh, priya and jordan you good to start?
[00:15] Jordan: yep good here, thanks Marcus. we saw the initial perf numbers you sent, curious about the gaps at 95th perc latency when load spikes, and how to keep costs down.
[00:30] Sofia: cool, so today we'll go through continuous batching behaviour first, then scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and token caps, and then kv cache/quantization tradeoffs. i'll also outline what we recommend for a 24 hour stress run.
[00:46] Priya: sound good. quick infra context, we're on GCP, using a mix of a2-highgpu and a4 pools for inference, and we want to keep p95 under 220ms for short completions (~40 tokens) and cost below our current self-host baseline.
[01:05] Diego: got it. two quick clarifications: are those completions single-shot or multi-turn chat? affects kv cache behavior.
[01:12] Priya: mostly single-shot, but we have a small percentage of multi-turn — like 5-10% where we cache previous context.
[01:20] Sofia: ok that matters. continuous batching in Redwood's runtime will try to batch small requests together to increase GPU utilization, but there's a tradeoff: batching increases tail latency if the scheduler waits too long for batch fills. our scheduler knobs let you tune that.
[01:38] Marcus: i'll pull up the recommended profile we use for latency-sensitive workloads — it's in the benchmarking sheet i shared.
[01:45] (link shared: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/brightscale-profile)
[01:52] Jordan: i noticed in the initial run the p95 jumped during a traffic spike even though avg tokens/sec was stable. what are we missing?
[02:05] Sofia: most likely the scheduler's batch-fill timeout or max_num_seqs setting. if max_num_seqs is too high, you get more packing but each sequence is longer and kv cache pressure increases; if the timeout is too large, single small requests sit waiting. we usually set max_num_seqs between 4-8 for short requests.
[02:28] Priya: we had max_num_seqs at 16 in our first run because we prioritized throughput. that explains it.
[02:35] Diego: also token limits — if you have a global token cap per batch that aligns poorly with token distribution, you can get partial batches and uneven latencies.
[02:45] Marcus: can you explain the interaction between continuous batching and kv cache evictions? i.e., when do we see more misses?
[02:55] Sofia: sure. continuous batching groups requests across concurrent sequences; for multi-turn flows, the runtime stores KV cache per session. if batches pack many different sessions with long sequences, the total KV size per batch grows and can exceed the per-GPU cache threshold, leading to evictions and reloading — spikes in latency. smaller max_num_seqs reduces per-batch kv footprint. also quantization can reduce memory per token so higher packing is possible.
[03:23] Evan: so quantization helps with kv size, but what about quality? we can't accept regressions in our completion accuracy for classification tasks.
[03:30] Sofia: right — we typically recommend post-training 4-bit quantization (int4-like) with quality checks. for BrightScale's models (you mentioned mixing a couple of open models), we can run an eval harness to measure delta on key prompts. often the delta is negligible for generation quality at lower lengths; for classification you need to validate.
[03:53] Jordan: okay. can you share a concrete set of knob values you recommend for our workload?
[04:00] Sofia: yes, start with: continuous batching enabled, scheduler.batch_fill_timeout_ms = 8-12ms, scheduler.max_num_seqs = 6, max_tokens_per_batch = 2048, and per-request token_limit = 128. For the 5-10% multi-turn flows, pin per-session kv retention to 60s in the pilot to avoid evictions.
[04:25] Priya: interesting, our current batch_fill is 25ms and max_num_seqs 16. that'll explain the p95 spikes.
[04:33] Diego: smaller timeout reduces waiting but increases number of micro-batches — can affect throughput. it's a tradeoff. we'll show you both throughput and p95 trade curves.
[04:44] Jordan: what about scheduler priority rules? we have a mix of realtime (low token completions) and background jobs (longer summaries).
[04:54] Marcus: you can tag routes; runtime will route realtime to low-latency pools with tighter batch timeouts and lower max_num_seqs, while background routes go to high-util pools with batching optimized for throughput. that's where Dedicated or Dedicated burst capacity helps.
[05:10] Priya: on Dedicated — does Redwood support pinning specific GPUs to routes? we want predictable performance for realtime.
[05:18] Sofia: yes, Dedicated lets you reserve pools and assign routing policies so realtime traffic hits nodes with reserved capacity. that reduces noisy neighbor risks.
[05:27] Evan: back to KV, where are those caches kept? memory on the GPU or host? eviction cost?
[05:33] Sofia: KV cache is primarily GPU memory when using native kernels. eviction requires reloading from host or re-computing, which is expensive. that's why reducing per-batch kv footprint via max_num_seqs is important. also quantization of KV structures reduces memory.
[05:49] Jordan: do you have metrics to show how p95 changes as we vary max_num_seqs?
[05:55] Sofia: yes — we pulled a quick micro-benchmark: with 40-token requests at same QPS, p95 was ~190ms with max_num_seqs=4 and batch_fill=10ms; p95 rose to ~360ms with max_num_seqs=16 and batch_fill=25ms, though throughput increased by ~1.6x. i'll attach the curves.
[06:17] Marcus: (shares link) https://redwood.example/benchmarks/throughput-curves
[06:24] Priya: we need the p99 too — our SLA looks at p99.
[06:27] Sofia: fair. p99 shows similar trends: it gets worse faster with large max_num_seqs because of outlier evictions. for p99-sensitive workloads, we bias for lower packing.
[06:40] Evan: any recommendations on dynamic knobs — can we auto-adjust based on queue depth?
[06:46] Sofia: yes — Redwood runtime has adaptive batching heuristics. you can enable adaptive mode where batch_fill_timeout scales down as queue length drops and increases under heavy load. but we still recommend conservative max_num_seqs for realtime.
[07:00] Jordan: curious on token caps — you recommended max_tokens_per_batch=2048 — is that per GPU?
[07:06] Diego: it's per-batch; if a GPU runs multiple batches concurrently (rare for large models) we account for that in capacity. the key is to set that cap to your typical avg token length * max_num_seqs and leave headroom.
[07:19] Priya: our average token length is ~42, 95th ~120. so with max_num_seqs 6 that's around 720 tokens typical, well below 2048.
[07:28] Marcus: perfect. that gives room for mixed requests without partial batches blowing up latency.
[07:33] Jordan: what about tokenization differences across models — we use two models with different tokenizer behaviour. does that affect batching decisions?
[07:40] Sofia: yes — runtime normalizes token counts at request admission based on model choice; we prefer route-level configs so requests for different tokenizers go to different pools or have per-route token caps.
[07:51] Evan: network — if we're on VPC/Private deployment, are there extra latencies?
[07:55] Diego: minimal; VPC adds a few ms depending on routing and NAT. the bigger issue is egress bandwidth and firewall rules causing occasional stalls. ensure health probes and keepalives are allowed.
[08:06] Priya: security stuff — SSO, KMS, audit logs — we need SOC2 docs and KMS integration details for data-in-transit and at rest.
[08:13] Marcus: i'll share SOC2 summary and our KMS integration guide. for private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs for rollout traces.
[08:24] Jordan: great. ok back to tuning: can we walk through a sample scheduler profile you will apply for the pilot?
[08:31] Sofia: yep, profile name: brightscale-latency-1. settings: continuous_batching: true, adaptive_batching: true, batch_fill_timeout_ms: 10, max_num_seqs: 6, max_tokens_per_batch: 2048, per_request_token_limit: 128, kv_retention_seconds: 60, quantization_profile: int4-balanced (pilot), fallback_policy: model_variant -> smaller model if queue > X.
[09:01] Priya: fallback_policy — if model variant changes, do we get semantic differences? we can't accept lower accuracy.
[09:09] Sofia: fallback should be used cautiously; for realtime we prefer to route to another region or reserved capacity first. variant fallbacks are for graceful degradation but require A/B validation.
[09:20] Jordan: what about batching at the SDK level — should we implement client-side batching to reduce variance?
[09:25] Diego: client batching helps but increases client-side latency — for small requests it's better to let runtime do continuous batching because it can pack across many clients. client-side batching can be used for background jobs.
[09:36] Evan: can you give an example failure mode we should watch for in the logs?
[09:40] Sofia: look for repeated KV cache reload messages, high host->gpu memcpy times, or frequent small batch counts with high GPU occupancy variance. we'll send SRE alert rules.
[09:50] Priya: nice — on quantization: you mentioned int4-balanced. do you have a test harness we can run to validate no perf regression on our classification suite?
[09:58] Marcus: yes, we'll provide a reproducible eval harness and an example notebook to compute delta metrics. we'll also run a quick sample on your key prompts during the pilot.
[10:10] Jordan: for the 24-hour throughput test, what metrics will you gather?
[10:14] Sofia: we'll log per-route QPS, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, batch sizes distribution, kv cache hit/miss rates, memory pressure, and token counts per batch. also track any evictions and serialization/deserialization times.
[10:28] Diego: we'll also produce a cost estimate for the pilot — tokens served, GPU hours, and expected unit economics vs your current self-host baseline.
[10:36] Priya: good. what's the expected uplift in throughput when we tighten max_num_seqs vs loosen it?
[10:41] Sofia: tightening reduces throughput but improves tail latency. typical trade: at our microbench, throughput drops ~20-30% between max_num_seqs 16 -> 6, while p95 improves ~40-50%. numbers depend on token distribution.
[10:56] Jordan: okay. i want to talk about the scheduler internals briefly — is batching synchronous or do you use an async scheduler?
[11:03] Diego: async event-driven scheduler. it collects inflight requests, applies admission control, and triggers kernel execution. batching decisions happen on admission and can be updated by adaptive heuristics.
[11:18] Evan: suppose we have a sudden burst from our web tier — how fast does the runtime scale?
[11:24] Sofia: autoscaling is policy-driven. for Dedicated you get reserved baseline capacity and autoscale for bursts. we recommend adding a small buffer (10-15%) to prevent cold starts affecting p99. scaling latency depends on provisioning model; if using pre-warmed instances scaling is a few seconds, otherwise it's minutes.
[11:40] Jordan: pre-warmed instances — is that part of Dedicated?
[11:42] Marcus: yes, Dedicated supports pre-warmed nodes for predictable scale.
[11:46] Priya: network egress costs matter — if you route across regions for fallback that's expensive.
[11:52] Diego: agreed, that's why we route by region first and only fallback regionally if configured. we'll include cost delta in the estimate.
[12:01] (brief pause, small cross-talk)
[12:10] Sofia: a few gotchas we've seen: 1) when customers enable both adaptive batching and high max_num_seqs, heuristics can overpack; 2) some models with long context windows are extremely KV-heavy; 3) client retries can create microbursts that break batching assumptions.
[12:29] Priya: on retries — we have a retry policy at the client for idempotent calls — should we adjust it?
[12:34] Sofia: yes, add jitter and exponential backoff to reduce synchronized retries. also add an ingress rate-limiter to smooth bursts.
[12:43] Jordan: let's talk about measuring optimal max_num_seqs — do you do an automated sweep?
[12:47] Sofia: we recommend a grid search during the pilot: run profiles with max_num_seqs in [4,6,8,12,16], batch_fill_timeout in [6,10,15,25ms], and track p95/p99/throughput. we'll run the sweep overnight and produce the Pareto frontier.
[13:05] Marcus: we'll set up the benchmark harness to replay your traces with token distribution. Priya, can you confirm you'll share traces?
[13:11] Priya: yes, we'll anonymize and share a 12-hour sample by Monday.
[13:15] Evan: what about KV warmup — if we pre-warm sessions can we avoid evictions?
[13:20] Sofia: you can pin sessions to nodes for short periods, but that reduces overall utilization. alternate option is a hot-key cache for top sessions. depends on access patterns.
[13:31] Jordan: any concerns about running the pilot on our VPC with private deployment?
[13:35] Diego: just ensure your private subnets have the required firewall ports open and that any corporate proxies don't mangle websocket or long-polling if you use streaming. we'll provide a checklist.
[13:46] Marcus: i'll include the VPC checklist with the SOC2 doc.
[13:50] Priya: ok. can we briefly go through an example log trace to identify KV cache eviction?
[13:55] Sofia: sure, example: [KVCache] session_id=abc123 eviction_reason=memory_pressure old_size=1.2G new_alloc=300M reload_time_ms=1245 — that reload_time is your worst-case spike. if you see repeated reloads correlated with p99 spikes, you need to reduce per-batch kv or increase node memory.
[14:24] Evan: 1245ms is huge. we can't have that.
[14:27] Sofia: right, that's why we aim to avoid evictions for realtime. sometimes we use smaller packed batches or bump instance types (more GPU memory) for those sessions.
[14:36] Jordan: cost vs performance — what's the typical incremental cost to bump instance type vs lower packing?
[14:42] Diego: rough rule: increasing GPU memory (next SKU) can add 20-30% cost but preserves throughput. lowering packing reduces throughput and increases unit cost per token, but may be cheaper than higher SKU depending on utilization. we'll model for your QPS.
[14:58] Priya: let's ensure the pilot captures those delta economics.
[15:02] Marcus: agreed. we'll produce a cost model.
[15:05] (short check-in, people typing)
[15:17] Sofia: another lever is KV quantization — we compress keys/values which reduces memory but adds small CPU/GPU overhead on unpack. good middle ground for some workloads.
[15:29] Jordan: any constraints around offloading KV to host memory?
[15:33] Sofia: offloading reduces GPU memory pressure but increases latency per token due to PCIe or NVLink transfers. only recommended for background jobs where latency constraints are looser.
[15:45] Priya: what about multi-GPU attention kernels — do those affect batching?
[15:49] Diego: multi-GPU kernels help for very large models; they change memory and compute patterns. for small 40-token requests multi-GPU rarely helps; it can increase latency due to interconnect synchronization.
[16:02] Jordan: good to know. ok let's talk about observability — what dashboards will you share?
[16:07] Marcus: per-route dashboards with p50/p95/p99, batch_size distribution, kv hit/miss, GPU mem pressure, and a trace view to correlate requests to kernel times. we'll give you Grafana links for the pilot.
[16:20] Evan: can we set alerts on kv miss rate > 5% or p99 > 500ms?
[16:25] Sofia: yes, we can suggest alert thresholds; your SRE can tune.
[16:29] Priya: next, testing quantized model — will Redwood host both variants and switch?
[16:35] Marcus: yes, we can host both and run canary comparisons. we recommend holding traffic split to 1% initially for validation.
[16:42] Jordan: about scheduler logs — can we get detailed admission logs for the pilot?
[16:47] Diego: yes, but they're verbose. we'll provide a sample and a compacted CSV with batch id, batch size, token_count, kv_mem_bytes, and latency.
[16:58] Priya: perfect. how long do you need from our side to get started?
[17:02] Marcus: if we get traces and confirm firewall/VPC checklist this week, our SE can run the sweep next week and share results by 12/16.
[17:10] Jordan: sounds good. any final questions from BrightScale?
[17:14] Evan: only one — do you support GPU-specific kernel tuning per model?
[17:19] Sofia: yes, our compilation stage picks kernels by model, seq-len distribution and hardware. we can also force specific kernel bundles for experiments.
[17:28] Priya: ok that's it from me. thanks.
[17:31] Marcus: great, recap and next steps: Marcus to share benchmark config and SOC2 + VPC checklist; Sofia to run bench sweep with suggested profiles and share curves; Priya to send traces and firewall confirmation; we'll reconvene week of 12/20.
[17:47] Jordan: thanks all.
[17:50] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: some product names transcribed as "redwood" variations; occasional filler words removed for readability, timestamps approximate.
